method_snippets.quote: Participants for the present randomized substudy were drawn from a larger mixed-sex cohort enrolled in the single-group parent project registered as NCT06435130.

The parent record describes the broader multi-phase study, whereas this manuscript reports a nested two-arm randomized comparison restricted to women with prediabetes who completed a 12-week juice-only protocol; no separate registration was created for this substudy.
Following eligibility screening, 54 women met the inclusion criteria and were enrolled in this study.
Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either the intervention group (IG) (n = 27) or the control group (CG) (n = 27) using a computer-generated randomization sequence.

Accordingly, the randomized between-group contrast represented the addition of chokeberry juice to the same Mediterranean diet recommendations rather than a comparison of two different background diets.

The present randomized controlled trial found that, in women with prediabetes advised to follow Mediterranean diet principles, adding 100 mL/day of chokeberry (Aronia melanocarpa) juice for 12 weeks was associated with greater improvements in glycemic control and systemic redox-related indices than Mediterranean diet recommendations alone.
Evidence from randomized trials with purified anthocyanins also supports a potential effect on glucose regulation, although findings are not uniform.

In a 12-week randomized placebo-controlled trial involving 160 adults with prediabetes or early untreated diabetes, 320 mg/day of purified anthocyanins resulted in a modest reduction in HbA1c compared with placebo [20].

All participants provided written informed consent.
Both were randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter trials evaluating canagliflozin in patients with T2DM.
In CANVAS, participants were randomized (1:1:1) to receive canagliflozin 300 mg, canagliflozin 100 mg or placebo.
In CREDENCE, randomization was (1:1) to receive canagliflozin 100 mg or placebo.
The primary outcome was the first UTI event, and the secondary outcome was total (first and recurrent) UTI events.

Three models were applied: Model 1 (unadjusted); Model 2 [adjusted for age, sex and treatment group (canagliflozin vs placebo)]; and Model 3 (fully adjusted for race, cerebrovascular disease, diabetes duration, body mass index, HbA1c, eGFR, UACR and the use of diuretics and insulin).
The effects of canagliflozin (pooled doses) versus placebo on outcomes were evaluated with Cox and Andersen–Gill models adjusted for age and sex.

The treatments were delivered by clinical psychologists or psychiatrists exclusively allocated to either ST or CBT (n = 29 and n = 28) for a minimum of a year, trained in the particular approach by internationally renowned therapists and supervised monthly by experts in groups of four, separated by condition.
The primary outcome was the severity of depressive symptoms, assessed with the German version of Beck's Depression Inventory II (BDI‐II; Hautzinger et al.

method_snippets.quote: In the BOREAS and NOTUS pooled population, dupilumab, a human monoclonal antibody blocking interleukin-4/13 signaling, significantly reduced moderate exacerbations (defined as requiring systemic corticosteroid or antibiotic use) or severe exacerbations (defined as requiring hospitalization or an emergency department [ED] visit >24 hours, or resulting in death) by 31% (rate ratio [95% CI] vs placebo, 0.70 [0.58-0.86]; P <.001) in patients with COPD and type 2 inflammation.
Severe exacerbations were nominally reduced by 32% (rate ratio [95% CI] vs placebo, 0.67 [0.44-1.04]; P = .073).

Full study designs of BOREAS (NCT03930732) and NOTUS (NCT04456673), two phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials, have been previously described.19-21 In brief, the intention-to-treat (ITT) population included patients aged 40 to 80 years (BOREAS) or 40 to 85 years (NOTUS) with COPD, moderate-to-severe airflow obstruction (post-bronchodilator forced expiratory volume in 1 second/forced vital capacity <0.7), and type 2 inflammation (blood eosinophil count ≥300 cells/µL at screening) on stable inhaled therapy (inhaled corticosteroids/long-acting muscarinic antagonist [LAMA]/long-acting beta-2 agonist [LABA], or LAMA/LABA if inhaled corticosteroids were contraindicated) for ≥3 months before randomization.
Patients were randomized 1:1 to add-on dupilumab 300 mg or matched placebo every 2 weeks subcutan­eously for up to 52 weeks.

Baseline demographics and disease characteristics for the pooled ITT population (dupilumab: N = 938; placebo: N = 936), patients without an exacerbation event during the study (dupilumab: n = 600; placebo: n = 542), and patients with ≥ 1 severe exacerbation (dupilumab: n = 41; placebo: n = 60) or moderate exacerbation(s) only (dupilumab: n = 297; placebo: n = 334) during the study were similar across treatment arms and subgroups (Table 1 and Table S1).

In the pooled ITT population, 5.3% (50 of 938) of patients receiving dupilumab and 8.5% (80 of 936) of patients receiving placebo had 65 and 96 ED visits/hospital admissions, respectively, during the 52-week treatment period.
Dupilumab reduced ED visits/hospital admissions by 38% (rate ratio [95% CI] vs placebo, 0.62 [0.43-0.90]; P = .0121) (Figure 1).
Dupilumab also delayed the time to first ED visit/hospital admission, with a risk reduction of 45% (HR [95% CI] vs placebo, 0.55 [0.38-0.78]; P = .0010) (Figure 2).

method_snippets.quote: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide.1 Among patients with newly diagnosed non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), 25–30% present with unresectable stage III disease, a population with particularly challenging therapeutic management.2 The standard care of these patients is definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy (cCRT) followed by consolidation immunotherapy.3–6 However, ~10–20% cases of stage III NSCLC harbor epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) gene mutations, a molecular subset historically associated with resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors.7 The subgroup analysis of PACIFIC study showed that durvalumab consolidation after cCRT did not improve the progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) in patients with EGFR-mutated stage III NSCLC, compared to placebo.8–10 Recent landmark trials, including LAURA and POLESTAR, have demonstrated s
In parallel with conventional approaches, chemotherapy-sparing strategies combining EGFR TKIs with definitive radiotherapy (RT) have emerged as a promising paradigm.

In the FLAURA trial, third-generation EGFR-TKI therapy achieved an objective response rate (ORR) of 80% in advanced EGFR-mutated NSCLC, notably higher than the 47.3% ORR reported with chemotherapy in the IPASS trial.21,22 More recently, the NeoADAURA trial provided pathological evidence of deeper responses with osimertinib monotherapy compared with chemotherapy, demonstrating a major pathologic response rate of 25% versus 2% (P < 0.001).23 The third-generation EGFR-TKIs are currently the preferred regimens for patients with stage IV EGFR-mutated NSCLC.24–26 However, previous reports have indicated that EGFR-TKI use may be associated with an increased risk of radiation pneumonitis (RP).14,27 In the LAURA study, the incidence of radiation pneumonitis in the osimertinib group was similar to that in the placebo group (48% vs.

Despite these advances in metastatic disease, no randomized evidence has directly compared third-generation TKI plus RT combinations with cCRT in the curative-intent management of unresectable stage III EGFR-mutated NSCLC.
Finally, 43 randomized participants (experimental arm: n = 24; control arm: n = 19) constituted the intent-to-treat (ITT) population.

For “LAURA-like” set, the patients finished planned radiotherapy without progression, who met the eligibility criteria of the LAURA study, induction TKI and concurrent RT showed significant OS benefit (P = 0.03) and resulted in separation of the OS curves at the first follow-up, though only 17.6% of patients died in short-term follow-up, which was also confirmed in the RWD set with long-term data.

These findings represent the first report from a prospective randomized trial demonstrating a significant OS benefit with induction therapy using a third-generation TKI + RT cCRT in a post-randomization subgroup analysis.
Given the reduced sample size and the possibility of an overestimated treatment effect due to early stopping, these findings—although compelling—warrant cautious interpretation.

method_snippets.section: Older adults with an intellectual disability
method_snippets.quote: A small feasibility study suggested potential benefits but lacked statistical power [24], while a feasibility randomised trial in adults with intellectual disability in London UK, struggled to recruit sufficient participants and did not progress to a full trial [25].

The primary aim of this study was to assess the feasibility, acceptability, and procedures required in order to conduct a randomised controlled trial, and to determine whether the prespecified progression criteria for advancing to a full trial were met.

This was a two-arm, randomised feasibility study with 1:1 allocation, which was conducted in two regions of the United Kingdom: one Health and Social Care Trust in Northern Ireland and one Trust in London, England.

We randomly allocated them to either the MATILDA intervention plus usual care or usual care with three group recreational activities with other older adults with an intellectual disability (active control arm).
The primary outcome measures were feasibility outcomes (eligibility, recruitment, consent, randomisation, matching to community groups and mentors, attendance, retention, dropout).
Secondary outcome measures focused on the clinical outcomes (i.e., quality of life, anxiety, loneliness).
Both primary and secondary outcome measures were collated at baseline, 6- and 12-months post intervention.
Statutory and voluntary disability community groups helped to identify potential adults with an intellectual disability who met the inclusion criteria using a user-friendly information sheet.

method_snippets.quote: The main purpose of this study was to evaluate whether standard treatment plus omeprazole is cost-effective compared to standard treatment alone for the prevention of corrosive esophageal stricture, using data from our previous randomized controlled trial (RCT).

Twenty adult patients (12 males and 8 females; mean age 29.4 ± 6.6 years) with Zargar grade 2b and 3a corrosive esophageal injuries were randomized to either standard care (n = 10) or standard care plus omeprazole (n = 10).
Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to enrollment.
Finally, the small sample size and short follow-up period limited our ability to adequately evaluate the long-term safety profile of omeprazole.
In addition, although the intervention demonstrated a lower stricture rate, the small sample size resulted in wide confidence intervals around the treatment effect estimate.
